name: Omar Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a visiting brass teacher for the county music service, so I drive between five primary schools teaching trumpet and cornet, mostly in groups of four. Saturday nights I play trumpet in a big band at the dinner dances in the Grand Hotel. Sundays I play at chapel in the morning, and with the town silver band in the afternoon when there's a concert.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the kids who come in shy and leave blasting a scale down the corridor. The hard part is that the music service pays by the hour, term by term, and the council keeps trimming it. My wife Grace is a teaching assistant, we married last year, and we rent a terraced house near her mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, common sense won. People were getting carried away. At chapel and at the band I'd say we should get back to proper work and stop chasing gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the robots were never my problem. The council cut the music service budget in spring and my hours dropped from twenty-two a week to seventeen. The thing that worries me isn't a computer, it's a council budget meeting I'll never be invited to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the head teachers directly whether they'd pay for extra lessons outside the music service. I'd take private pupils on Saturday mornings in the chapel hall, which the minister has said I could use. And I'd keep playing the hotel, which is the steadiest money I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit stubborn about it. We'll manage, we always do, but managing gets tiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said "we'll manage". What does managing look like this winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heating on for two hours in the evening, not four. Grace makes packed lunches for both of us. We don't eat out, and Christmas presents are small this year, which both families understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your hours dropped again, who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first. My dad's a plumber with his own small business, and he's always said there's a van seat for me. I'd rather earn it than take money, so I'd go and work for him a couple of days a week.

say: **Common sense** won, and people were getting carried away.
We should get back to **proper work** and stop chasing gadgets.
think: My real worry is a **council budget** meeting, not a computer.
My hours already fell from **twenty-two to seventeen** a week this year.
do: Ask head teachers to pay for **extra lessons** directly.
Teach private pupils on Saturdays in the **chapel hall**.
feel: **Uneasy** and **stubborn**; managing is tiring but familiar.
S0.quote: The thing that worries me isn't a computer, it's a council budget meeting I'll never be invited to.
fieldNote: Even in AI Plateau, a **council cut** has already taken five hours a week.
He'd turn to **family work** before any public help.
He and his wife Grace are already **cutting back** on heating and Christmas.

steps.text: Ask head teachers to pay for extra brass lessons directly
Teach private trumpet pupils on Saturdays in the chapel hall
Keep the heating to two hours an evening this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no substitute for a teacher in the room with a child and an instrument. I'd say it to the head teachers and to anyone at chapel. I'm not one for online arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I can see the council buying an app instead of paying people like me. If the music service shrinks, the visiting teachers on hourly pay go first, and that's me. A council that can buy a brass tutor app for every school will cut a man on hourly pay without blinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start two days a week with my dad's plumbing business, learning the trade properly while I keep the teaching I still have. I'd keep the hotel band and the Saturday pupils. I wouldn't use the AI things; I'd rather do something with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I know where to go. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel working for your dad, after a music degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proud and a bit embarrassed, both. My dad paid for half my trumpet when I was fifteen, so he'd see it as getting a bit back. Grace would be relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should be helping people through this, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families and churches first, and businesses taking on apprentices. I don't want the government paying people to sit at home. I'd want them to make it easier for small firms like my dad's to hire.

I'd tell **head teachers** and people at chapel, not argue online.

**Hourly-paid** visiting teachers go first, and that's me.

Keep the **hotel band** and the Saturday pupils.
Avoid **AI tools** and work with my hands instead.
S1.quote: A council that can buy a brass tutor app for every school will cut a man on hourly pay without blinking.
fieldNote: His **family trade** is a ready fallback most musicians don't have.
He favours **apprenticeships** and small firms over state support.
Working for his dad brings both **pride** and embarrassment.

steps.text: Work two days a week learning plumbing with his dad
Keep Saturday nights with the hotel big band
Lean on his dad's business while teaching hours shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after our own: families, chapels, neighbours. I'd say the government should help small firms keep people on, not just hand out cheques. And I'd say it at chapel, where people would be frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and the music service is gone, and so is half of what Grace does as a teaching assistant, because the marking and reading help go to computers. The hotel band lasts until the robots, around 2031, if people still have money for dinner dances. My wife Grace and I could both be out of school jobs by 2028, and my trumpet won't pay the rent on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time with my dad straight away and start a proper plumbing apprenticeship. We'd give up the rented house and move in with Grace's mum, who has a spare room. I'd sell the second trumpet and the flugelhorn, maybe nine hundred together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Sick in the stomach, if I'm honest, but I'd keep it off my face at chapel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come about three years later. Doesn't that reach plumbing too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I don't believe a robot will be under someone's sink in an old terraced house by 2031. Those pipes are all different. If I'm wrong, at least I'll have had three years of wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you pray for, if you don't mind me asking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for things to go back; I don't think they would. For Grace to keep her nerve and for my dad's business to hold. And that people still want a trumpet at Christmas.

say: We need to **look after our own**: families, chapels and neighbours.
The government should help **small firms** keep people on, not hand out cheques.
think: Grace and I could both lose **school jobs** by 2028.
The **hotel band** lasts only if people can still afford dinner dances.
do: Go **full-time** with my dad and start a plumbing apprenticeship.
Move in with **Grace's mum** to give up the rent.
Sell the second trumpet and **flugelhorn** for about nine hundred.
feel: **Alarmed** and sick, but he'd keep it **off his face** at chapel.
S2.quote: My wife Grace and I could both be out of school jobs by 2028, and my trumpet won't pay the rent on its own.
fieldNote: Both household incomes sit in **schools**, so the fast scenario hits twice.
He doubts robots can handle **old pipes** by 2031, but admits he could be wrong.
**Faith and family** shape both his plan and his public message.

steps.text: Start a full-time plumbing apprenticeship with his dad
Move into Grace's mum's spare room to give up the rent
Sell the spare trumpet and flugelhorn for about nine hundred
Lean on chapel and family for support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time enough for anyone willing to work, and we shouldn't wait for the government to fix it. I'd tell the older lads in the silver band to get a trade behind them. At chapel I'd say we'd look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd want to keep teaching as long as there were lessons, and that could be my mistake. The music service would shrink every year until 2031. With five years, I'd probably keep teaching trumpet till the council sends the final letter, and only then go to my dad's van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the plumbing course part-time at the college, evenings, about seven hundred a year, while I keep teaching. Grace and I would save what we can, maybe seventy a month. I'd keep the hotel and the band.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy most days, and alarmed when I let myself think about Grace's job too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said that could be your mistake. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm a teacher and a trumpet player, and I trained for it. I don't like change, never have. Grace says I'd wait until the house was on fire to buy a smoke alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Grace do in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's thought about training as a nursery nurse, because little ones need a real person. We'd want children in a few years, and that would make her want to stay close to small kids anyway. We'd have to plan that carefully.

The older lads in the band should get a **trade** behind them.
think: I'd keep teaching until the **final letter**, which may be a mistake.
The **music service** shrinks every year until 2031.

fieldNote: He openly admits he'd **wait too long**, as Grace teases him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who doesn't prepare has only themselves to blame. That sounds hard, but it's what I believe. I'd also say chapels and families should be ready to help the ones who struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd be thirty-seven, and hands-on work goes on till about 2039. Teaching shrinks before that, I'm sure. Ten years is long enough for me to become a plumber who plays trumpet, instead of a trumpet player who can't pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the plumbing qualification over three years, evenings, and drop teaching gradually. I'd keep the hotel band and chapel as long as I can lift a trumpet. And Grace and I would start trying for a baby in a couple of years, which we'd always planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still worried about money, but I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who don't prepare have themselves to blame. Would that include you, if you waited?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would, and I'd deserve to hear it. Grace would tell me first. That's partly why I'd sign up early in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your children, if you had them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade and an instrument, both. One to pay the bills and one to keep them sane. That's what my dad gave me, really.

**Chapels and families** should be ready to help those who struggle.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Grace and I both work in schools, so we'd both be in trouble at once. What would help is help for small businesses like my dad's to take on apprentices, so people can earn while they learn a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about chapel. When the minister asks me to play the last hymn at a funeral, nobody in that chapel wants a machine doing it.

headlineQuote: When the minister asks me to play the last hymn at a funeral, nobody in that chapel wants a machine doing it.
portrait: Omar is a **27-year-old trumpet player** who teaches brass in schools and plays a hotel big band.
He married Grace, a **teaching assistant**, last year, and they have almost **no savings**.
He **never uses AI**, values faith and family, and prefers apprenticeships to handouts.
His fallback in every scenario is his dad's **plumbing business**.
He admits he'd **wait too long** to act unless the warning is short or Grace pushes him.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he and Grace both work in schools.
whatWouldHelp: Support for **small businesses** like his dad's to take on **apprentices**.
